patient.name: Gloria Mensah
patient.complaint: Colicky central abdominal pain and vomiting for 1 day
background: Lives in Brixton; retired school cook

diagnosis.exam: Expect 'Which is the most likely diagnosis?' or 'most likely cause?': colicky pain with early vomiting and a surgical scar means adhesional small bowel obstruction; an older patient with weight loss and late vomiting means colorectal cancer; a quiet post-operative abdomen means ileus.

points: Gloria, 64, has **colicky central pain** coming in waves since yesterday.
She has **vomited six times**, now green fluid.
No bowels opened for 2 days; **no flatus** since this morning.

steps.lead: Gloria's gut contents are not getting through. First question: is something **blocking** the bowel, or has it stopped moving (**ileus**)?

visual.title: Where Gloria's pain is
visual.caption: Central, colicky, periumbilical pain is small bowel (midgut). Large bowel pain is often lower.

points: Abdomen **distended**, with a lower midline scar.
Mildly tender centrally; no guarding or rigidity.

steps.lead: Gloria has pain, vomiting, distension, **absolute constipation** and **tinkling** sounds: a mechanical obstruction, not ileus.

steps.q: Early vomiting, colicky central pain and a scar from previous surgery. Which is the most likely cause?
steps.r: **Adhesions** from previous surgery are the commonest cause of small bowel obstruction. Cancer is the commonest cause of large bowel obstruction.

steps.lead: Early vomiting and two old operations: Gloria has **adhesional small bowel obstruction**, the commonest pattern of all.

steps.title: Small bowel vs large bowel obstruction vs ileus
head: Feature
Small bowel
Large bowel
Ileus

steps.lead: Gloria's pain is still colicky and she has **no peritonism**, but every review must look for these **strangulation** red flags.

steps.text: A change from **colicky to constant** pain, with fever, tachycardia and a raised lactate, means the bowel is dying. Do not keep waiting with 'drip and suck'.

steps.lead: Gloria's hernial orifices are clear, but always check them: a **femoral hernia** can cause obstruction and strangulates easily.

steps.text: **Meconium ileus** (newborn, no meconium after 48 hours, bilious vomiting, 'bubbly' AXR) suggests **cystic fibrosis**.

investigation.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?' (CT abdomen and pelvis) or questions on AXR signs: valvulae conniventes for small bowel, Rigler sign for perforation.

steps.lead: Gloria's vomiting has dried her out. **FBC, U&Es, CRP and a VBG** show dehydration, AKI, electrolytes and lactate.

steps.title: Gloria's bloods and VBG
steps.text: Dehydrated with AKI and low potassium. A normal lactate makes ischaemia less likely, for now.

visual.title: Gloria's lactate
visual.label: Gloria 1.6
visual.caption: A rising lactate on repeat VBG is a strangulation red flag.

steps.lead: Gloria's AXR shows **central dilated loops** with lines crossing the full width: **valvulae conniventes**, so this is small bowel.

steps.title: Reading the AXR
head: Sign
Means
rows: **Perforation**: gas both sides of the bowel wall

steps.q: Which investigation will localise the site and cause of Gloria's obstruction?
steps.r: **CT abdomen and pelvis** is the gold standard: it finds the transition point, the cause and signs of ischaemia.

steps.lead: After her ABCDE assessment, Gloria's **CT** shows dilated small bowel to a **transition point** in the pelvis, with no closed loop.

steps.text: An AXR suggests obstruction but **CT is the gold standard**. Do not pick AXR when the question asks for the diagnostic test.

management.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate initial management?' (nil by mouth, NG tube, IV fluids) and 'next step' questions where red flags or failure to improve mean surgery.

steps.lead: Gloria gets **drip and suck**: nil by mouth, an **NG tube** to decompress her stomach and **IV fluids** with potassium.

steps.q: Gloria has adhesional SBO with no red flags. Which is the most appropriate initial management?
o: Nil by mouth, NG tube and IV fluids
steps.r: **Drip and suck**. Many adhesional obstructions settle without surgery. A flatus tube is a large bowel treatment.

steps.title: Gloria's obstruction pathway
nodes: NBM, NG tube, IV fluids, correct electrolytes
No red flags → conservative, review regularly
steps.caption: Reassess often: a quiet, settling abdomen is good; constant pain and a rising lactate are not.

visual.title: Gloria settles with drip and suck
visual.caption: Falling NG output and passing flatus on day 3 mean the obstruction is resolving.

steps.lead: Had Gloria developed constant pain, peritonism, a rising lactate or a **closed loop** on CT, she would go for **urgent surgery**.

steps.text: A **flatus tube** after sigmoidoscope decompression treats a large bowel cause such as sigmoid volvulus. It does nothing for small bowel obstruction.

steps.lead: If Gloria needed a laparotomy, a few days of **post-operative ileus** would be expected and managed **conservatively**.
Gloria's care follows guidance for the acute abdomen and acute bowel obstruction.

points: Day 3: passing flatus; NG output falling.
Day 4: NG tube out; sips, then light diet.
Potassium and creatinine back to normal.
Home day 6; told adhesional obstruction can recur.

science.exam: Expect applied questions: why obstruction causes colicky pain and tinkling sounds, why ileus is quiet, why closed-loop obstruction is dangerous and why patients become so dry.

steps.lead: Gloria's colicky waves and tinkling sounds are her bowel **pushing hard against the blockage**.
Had Gloria's bowel simply stopped moving (**ileus**), it would be silent and her pain dull, not colicky.

steps.q: A patient on day 2 after a colectomy has distension, vomiting and absent bowel sounds. Why are the sounds absent?
steps.r: **Ileus** is generalised failure of peristalsis from surgical handling, opioids, sepsis or low potassium.

steps.lead: Gloria's CT showed **no closed loop**. If two points had been blocked, pressure in the trapped loop would rise fast.

steps.title: Why closed loops perforate
nodes: Bowel blocked at two points (volvulus, narrow-necked hernia)

steps.lead: Gloria lost litres to vomiting and **third spacing**, explaining her AKI and low potassium.

steps.title: Where Gloria's fluid went
nodes: Fluid pooling in the dilated bowel lumen
Dehydration, AKI, low K and Na
steps.caption: This is why IV fluids with electrolyte replacement come before anything else.

mcq.q: Which is the most common cause of small bowel obstruction?
Which is the most common cause of large bowel obstruction in older adults?
Which bowel sounds suggest paralytic ileus?
In which obstruction does vomiting come early?
mcq.r: **Small bowel** obstruction vomits early; large bowel is constipated first.

mcq.q: Which is the gold-standard investigation for intestinal obstruction?
mcq.r: **CT abdomen and pelvis** localises the site and cause.

mcq.q: Which AXR feature identifies dilated small bowel?
mcq.r: **Valvulae conniventes** cross the full width: 'stacked coins'.
**Rigler (double wall) sign**: gas on both sides of the bowel wall.

o: IV fluids and NG tube, nil by mouth

mcq.q: Which finding mandates urgent surgery in bowel obstruction?
mcq.r: **Closed loop**, strangulation, ischaemia, perforation or failed conservative management.

mcq.q: Why does mechanical obstruction cause colicky pain?
mcq.r: **Increased peristalsis against the obstruction** until the bowel fatigues.

prompts.q: What is intestinal obstruction, what are its two broad types, and how does it present?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: the four cardinal features, then decide mechanical or ileus.

points.p: Failure of bowel contents to pass: mechanical obstruction or ileus (non-mechanical paralysis)
points.why: The bowel sounds tell them apart.

points.p: Abdominal pain, vomiting, distension
points.why: Three of the four cardinal features.

points.p: Absolute constipation and failure to pass flatus
points.why: Passing flatus argues against complete obstruction.

points.p: Dehydration and electrolyte disturbance
points.why: Losses from vomiting and third spacing.

prompts.q: How do small bowel obstruction, large bowel obstruction and ileus differ, and what is the commonest cause of each?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: timing of vomiting, character of pain, bowel sounds.

points.p: SBO: colicky pain, early vomiting, tinkling sounds
SBO commonest cause: adhesions (also hernia, Crohn's, tumour)
LBO: constipation before vomiting; commonest cause colorectal cancer (also volvulus, diverticular stricture)
points.why: Older patient with weight loss or change in bowel habit.

points.p: Ileus: post-operative, distended, vomiting, sluggish sounds, no colicky pain
points.why: Also sepsis, electrolytes, opioids, severe illness.

prompts.q: What are the red flags for strangulation, ischaemia or perforation in obstruction?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: colicky becoming constant is the turning point.

points.p: Severe constant pain
points.why: Colicky pain is the bowel working; constant pain is the bowel dying.

points.p: Fever and tachycardia
Localised peritonism or rigid abdomen
points.why: Needs urgent CT and possible laparotomy.

points.p: Raised lactate
Rigler sign (perforation) or thumbprinting (ischaemia) on imaging

prompts.q: What else can cause obstruction in special groups: newborns, Peutz-Jeghers, femoral hernia?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: each is tested by one signature clue.

points.p: Meconium ileus: no meconium after 48 hours, bilious vomiting, bubbly AXR without fluid levels
Peutz-Jeghers: pigmented oral/palm/sole lesions, obstruction by intussusception
points.why: Hamartomatous polyps act as lead points.

points.p: Femoral hernia: high incarceration/strangulation risk, may need emergency surgery

prompts.q: What are the first-line and gold-standard investigations for obstruction?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: bloods first, CT to diagnose.

points.p: FBC, U&Es, CRP, VBG
Gold standard: CT abdomen and pelvis
points.why: Shows site, cause, closed loop and ischaemia.

points.p: ABCDE and assess for acute abdomen/peritonitis first
points.why: Sick patients are stabilised before the scanner.

prompts.q: What does an AXR show in obstruction, and how do you tell small from large bowel?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: lines that cross the whole width are small bowel.

points.p: Small bowel identified by valvulae conniventes
points.why: They cross the full width of the bowel.

points.p: 'Stacked coins' or 'ladder' appearance of distended loops
Large bowel: haustra cross only part of the width, peripheral position

prompts.q: What is the initial management of small and large bowel obstruction?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: 'drip and suck' is the answer unless there is a red flag.

points.p: Nil by mouth
NG (Ryles) tube for decompression
IV fluids and correction of electrolytes
Treat the cause and surgical review
points.why: Adhesional SBO often settles without surgery.

points.p: LBO: flatus tube after sigmoidoscope decompression

prompts.q: When does obstruction need urgent surgery, and how is post-operative ileus managed?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: red flags or failure to settle mean theatre.

points.p: Strangulation or ischaemia
Perforation
Closed-loop obstruction
Failed conservative management
points.why: Persisting obstruction despite drip and suck.

points.p: Post-operative ileus: conservative, allow motility to recover

prompts.q: Why does mechanical obstruction cause colicky pain and tinkling sounds, while ileus is quiet?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: one is a working bowel against a block, the other a bowel that has stopped.

points.p: Proximal dilatation from trapped gas and fluid
Increased peristalsis against the obstruction until the bowel fatigues
points.why: Late obstruction can go quiet too.

points.p: Ileus: generalised failure of coordinated peristalsis (surgery, electrolytes, sepsis, opioids)
points.why: Hence reduced or absent sounds, less colicky pain.

prompts.q: Why is closed-loop obstruction dangerous, and why does obstruction cause major fluid loss?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: two blocked ends mean nowhere for pressure to go.

points.p: Closed loop: bowel obstructed at two points (volvulus, narrow-necked hernia)
Rapid pressure rise compromises blood supply and risks perforation
Strangulation: venous congestion then arterial occlusion → necrosis, perforation, faecal peritonitis, sepsis
Fluid loss from vomiting, bowel wall oedema, reduced intake and third spacing
points.why: Causes dehydration, AKI and electrolyte derangement.

glossary.ileus: Non-mechanical failure of bowel movement (paralysis), so contents do not pass although nothing blocks them.
glossary.paralytic ileus: Another name for ileus: the bowel stops contracting, typically after surgery.
glossary.mechanical obstruction: A physical blockage of the bowel lumen, such as adhesions, a hernia or a tumour.
glossary.obstipation: Severe constipation with no passage of stool or gas; absolute constipation.
glossary.flatus: Gas passed from the bowel through the anus.
glossary.adhesions: Bands of scar tissue inside the abdomen, usually after surgery, that can kink or trap bowel.
glossary.tinkling bowel sounds: High-pitched bowel sounds of fluid and gas forced past a mechanical blockage.
glossary.visible peristalsis: Waves of bowel contraction seen through a thin abdominal wall in obstruction.
glossary.peritonism: Signs of peritoneal irritation: guarding, rigidity, rebound and percussion tenderness.
glossary.strangulation: Loss of blood supply to a trapped segment of bowel, leading to ischaemia.
glossary.closed-loop obstruction: A bowel segment blocked at both ends, so pressure builds rapidly inside it.
glossary.Rigler sign: Gas seen on both sides of the bowel wall on X-ray; a sign of perforation.
glossary.thumbprinting: Thickened, scalloped bowel wall on imaging from oedema; suggests ischaemia.
glossary.valvulae conniventes: Mucosal folds of the small bowel that cross its full width on X-ray.
glossary.haustra: Pouches of the colon wall; on X-ray their folds cross only part of the bowel width.
glossary.stacked coins: AXR look of dilated small bowel with valvulae conniventes, like a pile of coins.
glossary.transition point: The point on CT where dilated bowel changes to collapsed bowel; the site of obstruction.
glossary.NG tube: Nasogastric tube: passed through the nose into the stomach to drain contents.
glossary.Ryles tube: A wide-bore nasogastric tube used to decompress the stomach.
glossary.drip and suck: Conservative obstruction care: IV fluids (drip) and NG tube drainage (suck), nil by mouth.
glossary.NBM: Nil by mouth: nothing to eat or drink.
glossary.flatus tube: A soft tube passed into the rectum to let gas out of a distended large bowel.
glossary.VBG: Venous blood gas: a quick test for pH, lactate, potassium and bicarbonate.
glossary.lactate: A product of anaerobic metabolism; raised levels suggest tissue ischaemia.
glossary.third spacing: Fluid shifting out of the blood into the bowel lumen and wall, where it cannot be used.
glossary.AKI: Acute kidney injury: a rapid fall in kidney function, shown by rising creatinine.
glossary.meconium ileus: Newborn bowel obstruction from thick meconium, strongly linked to cystic fibrosis.
glossary.meconium: A newborn's first stool, normally passed within 48 hours.
glossary.Peutz-Jeghers syndrome: Inherited hamartomatous gut polyps with dark freckles on lips, palms and soles.
glossary.intussusception: One segment of bowel telescoping into the next, causing obstruction.
glossary.volvulus: Twisting of a loop of bowel on its mesentery, causing closed-loop obstruction.
glossary.laparotomy: An open abdominal operation through a large incision.
glossary.Hartmann's procedure: Sigmoid resection with an end colostomy and closed rectal stump.
glossary.ABCDE: The structured emergency assessment: Airway, Breathing, Circulation, Disability, Exposure.
glossary.bilious vomiting: Green vomit containing bile, suggesting obstruction beyond the ampulla.

technique.stem: A 58 year old man has a 1 day history of colicky central abdominal pain and repeated vomiting. He has not passed stool or flatus for 12 hours. He had a laparotomy for a perforated duodenal ulcer 6 years ago. His abdomen is distended with a midline scar and high-pitched tinkling bowel sounds. There is no guarding.
technique.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

steps.x: Diagnosis: obstruction or not, then small or large bowel, then cause.
Four cardinal features with early vomiting, central colic and a previous laparotomy.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Small bowel obstruction**, most likely adhesional.

elim: Pancreatitis gives epigastric pain to the back, no absolute constipation.
LBO has constipation first and late vomiting.
Ileus has absent, not tinkling, bowel sounds.
Volvulus causes massive distension with late vomiting, often in the elderly.

steps.x: **E. Small bowel obstruction.** Rule: scar + colic + early vomiting = adhesional SBO.

technique.stem: A 71 year old woman has 2 days of colicky abdominal pain, vomiting and distension. She had an open hysterectomy 20 years ago. Her pulse rate is 104 bpm and BP 118/72 mmHg. An abdominal X-ray shows dilated central loops of bowel with folds crossing their full width. She has been given IV fluids and an NG tube.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?

steps.x: 'Diagnostic' means the test that confirms site and cause.
AXR already suggests SBO (valvulae conniventes); now find the site, cause and any ischaemia.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **CT abdomen and pelvis** is the gold standard.

elim: Repeating the AXR adds nothing diagnostic.
Barium can impact and is dangerous if perforated.
MRI is slow and used for Crohn's, not acute obstruction.
Gas-filled bowel blocks the ultrasound view.

steps.x: **C. CT abdomen and pelvis.** Rule: AXR suggests, CT confirms.

technique.stem: A 66 year old woman has 1 day of colicky central abdominal pain, bilious vomiting and distension. She had an appendicectomy and a caesarean section. Her pulse rate is 100 bpm and BP 122/74 mmHg. Her abdomen is distended but soft, with tinkling bowel sounds. CT shows adhesional small bowel obstruction with no closed loop or ischaemia.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
o: Nil by mouth, NG tube and IV fluids

steps.x: Initial management: is there any red flag forcing surgery?
Uncomplicated adhesional SBO, normal lactate, no peritonism.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Drip and suck**: NBM, NG tube, IV fluids, correct electrolytes.

elim: No red flags; many adhesional SBOs settle without surgery.
Laxatives do not pass a blockage and worsen vomiting.
A flatus tube is for large bowel causes such as volvulus.
Colonoscopy has no role in SBO.

steps.x: **B.** Rule: uncomplicated SBO = drip and suck, review often.

technique.stem: A 62 year old man has 12 hours of severe abdominal pain and vomiting. CT shows a loop of small bowel trapped in a narrow-necked internal hernia, obstructed at both its entry and exit points, with a thickened wall. The surgeon books him for immediate laparotomy rather than conservative management.
technique.q: Which is the most likely reason this obstruction needs urgent surgery?
o: Rapid pressure rise in a segment obstructed at two points

steps.x: Mechanism: why is this obstruction an emergency?

clues: obstructed at both its entry and exit points
steps.x: A closed loop, already showing wall changes.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Closed loop: **pressure rises fast**, blood supply fails, perforation follows.

elim: Translocation follows ischaemia; it is not the primary reason.
Opioids cause ileus, not a closed loop.
Fluid loss occurs in all obstruction and is treated with fluids.
Alkalosis is corrected medically, not surgically.

steps.x: **B.** Rule: closed loop = theatre.

practice.stem: A 59 year old woman has a 1 day history of colicky central abdominal pain and bilious vomiting. She has not passed flatus since this morning. She had an open hysterectomy 15 years ago. Her temperature is 37.1°C, pulse rate 102 bpm and BP 116/72 mmHg. Her abdomen is distended with tinkling bowel sounds. Hernial orifices are clear.
practice.q: Which is the most likely cause?
practice.e: Small bowel obstruction after previous abdominal surgery is most likely adhesional. Hernial orifices are clear, so a hernia is less likely.

steps.x: Cause of obstruction: first decide small or large bowel.

clues: colicky central abdominal pain and bilious vomiting
steps.x: SBO with a previous operation and no hernia.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Adhesions**, the commonest cause of SBO.

elim: No history of Crohn's disease.
Gallstone ileus is rare, in elderly with biliary disease and pneumobilia.
The hernial orifices are clear.
Lymphoma is rare, with weight loss and B symptoms.

steps.x: **A. Adhesions.** Rule: scar + SBO = adhesions.

practice.stem: A 78 year old man has a 4 day history of increasing abdominal distension and colicky lower abdominal pain. He has not opened his bowels for 4 days and started vomiting today. He has lost 6 kg over 3 months and noticed his stools becoming looser. He has never had abdominal surgery. His abdomen is tympanic with tinkling bowel sounds.
practice.q: Which is the most likely cause?
practice.e: Large bowel obstruction (constipation before vomiting) with weight loss and change in bowel habit in an older man is colorectal carcinoma, the commonest LBO cause.

steps.x: Cause: small or large bowel, then the commonest cause for that level.

clues: not opened his bowels for 4 days and started vomiting today
steps.x: Constipation first, late vomiting = LBO; weight loss and bowel habit change = malignancy.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Colorectal carcinoma.**

elim: No previous surgery, and adhesions cause SBO.
Caecal volvulus is sudden, without weight loss.
A diverticular stricture follows recurrent diverticulitis.
Impaction would be felt on rectal exam, no weight loss.

steps.x: **C. Colorectal carcinoma.** Rule: LBO in older adults = cancer until proven otherwise.

practice.stem: A 70 year old woman is 3 days after a right hemicolectomy. She has abdominal distension and has vomited twice. She has not passed flatus. She is on a morphine PCA. Her abdomen is distended, mildly tender around the wound, and silent on auscultation. There is no colicky pain. Her temperature is 37.0°C, pulse rate 88 bpm and BP 128/76 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Post-operative distension, vomiting and absent bowel sounds without colicky pain, with opioids and low potassium, is paralytic ileus. Mechanical obstruction gives colicky pain and tinkling sounds.

steps.x: Post-operative distension: mechanical or ileus?
Post-op, opioids, low potassium, silent abdomen, no colic, stable observations.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Paralytic ileus.**

elim: Mechanical SBO gives colicky pain and tinkling sounds.
A leak causes fever, tachycardia and peritonitis.
LBO also causes colic and tinkling sounds.
Toxic megacolon follows colitis, with systemic toxicity.

steps.x: **D. Paralytic ileus.** Rule: silent + no colic + post-op = ileus.

practice.stem: A 65 year old man admitted with adhesional small bowel obstruction 24 hours ago now has severe constant abdominal pain. His temperature is 38.4°C, pulse rate 124 bpm and BP 102/64 mmHg. He has guarding and percussion tenderness in the right lower abdomen. His NG tube is draining well.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Colicky pain becoming constant with fever, tachycardia, localised peritonism and a lactate of 5.1 means strangulation. It needs urgent surgery.

steps.x: A change in a known obstruction: has it become complicated?
Every strangulation red flag plus lactate 5.1.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Strangulated small bowel obstruction.**

elim: Biliary colic is RUQ pain without obstruction or lactate rise.
Mesenteric adenitis is a mild illness in the young.
Ileus is painless and quiet.
Simple obstruction does not cause fever, peritonism and a high lactate.

steps.x: **E. Strangulated SBO.** Next: urgent laparotomy.

practice.stem: A 2 day old boy has not passed meconium since birth. He has bilious vomiting and a distended abdomen. His older sister has cystic fibrosis. An abdominal X-ray shows dilated loops of bowel with a 'bubbly' appearance in the right lower abdomen and no air-fluid levels.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Failure to pass meconium beyond 48 hours with bilious vomiting, a bubbly AXR without fluid levels and a family history of cystic fibrosis is meconium ileus.

steps.x: Neonatal obstruction: the X-ray and the family history decide.
Delayed meconium, CF link, bubbly AXR.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Meconium ileus.**

elim: Duodenal atresia gives a 'double bubble' and is linked to Down syndrome.
Hirschsprung's also delays meconium but lacks the CF link and bubbly pattern.
Malrotation presents with sudden bilious vomiting, often after passing meconium.
NEC affects preterm babies, with bloody stools and pneumatosis.

steps.x: **D. Meconium ileus.** Then test for cystic fibrosis.

practice.stem: A 60 year old man has a 2 day history of colicky central abdominal pain and vomiting. He had a laparotomy after a stab wound 10 years ago. His abdomen is distended with tinkling bowel sounds. An abdominal X-ray is requested.
practice.q: Which is the most likely finding on the abdominal X-ray?
o: Haustra crossing part of the bowel width
Valvulae conniventes crossing the full bowel width
practice.e: Adhesional SBO shows dilated central loops with valvulae conniventes ('stacked coins'). Haustra mark large bowel; Rigler sign means perforation.

steps.x: Finding question: name the diagnosis, then its X-ray sign.

clues: colicky central abdominal pain and vomiting
steps.x: Adhesional small bowel obstruction.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Dilated small bowel with **valvulae conniventes**.

elim: Bubbly without fluid levels is meconium ileus in a newborn.
Coffee bean is sigmoid volvulus.
Haustra mean large bowel dilatation.
Rigler sign means perforation; he has no peritonism.

steps.x: **E.** Rule: full-width folds = small bowel.

practice.stem: A 68 year old woman has 2 days of colicky abdominal pain, vomiting, distension and absolute constipation. She had a laparoscopic cholecystectomy and an open appendicectomy in the past. She has been resuscitated with IV fluids and an NG tube has been passed. Her abdomen is distended but not peritonitic.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?
practice.e: CT abdomen and pelvis is the gold standard: it localises the site and cause of obstruction and looks for ischaemia. AXR only suggests obstruction.

steps.x: 'Diagnostic' = gold standard.
Suspected obstruction, now stable enough to scan.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **CT abdomen and pelvis.**

elim: Gas-filled bowel blocks ultrasound.
AXR suggests obstruction but cannot show cause or ischaemia.
Erect CXR looks only for free gas.
Contrast enema assesses only the colon.

steps.x: **C. CT abdomen and pelvis.**

practice.stem: A 74 year old man with small bowel obstruction from adhesions has been managed with NG drainage and IV fluids for 12 hours. The nurse reports his pain has changed from colicky to constant. His temperature is 37.9°C and pulse rate 112 bpm. The surgical team want a quick bedside test for bowel ischaemia.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?
practice.e: A VBG gives a rapid lactate, which rises with bowel ischaemia, plus potassium and pH. CRP is slow and non-specific.

steps.x: A quick bedside test for ischaemia.

clues: quick bedside test for bowel ischaemia
steps.x: Possible strangulation; you need lactate now.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **VBG** for lactate (then urgent CT and surgical review).

elim: Amylase is for pancreatitis.
CRP is slow and non-specific for ischaemia.
D-dimer is non-specific and not a bedside ischaemia test.
Troponin is for myocardial injury.

steps.x: **E. Venous blood gas.** Rule: lactate is the ischaemia marker.

practice.stem: A 63 year old woman is admitted with adhesional small bowel obstruction. She has an NG tube on free drainage and is nil by mouth. Her pulse rate is 98 bpm and BP 120/74 mmHg. Her abdomen is soft and not peritonitic. CT shows no closed loop or ischaemia.
practice.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
practice.e: Drip and suck includes correcting electrolytes: she is dry and hypokalaemic, so IV fluids with added potassium. Oral replacement is useless while she is NBM with NG drainage.

steps.x: Next step in a patient already on NG drainage.
Uncomplicated SBO with potassium 2.9 and raised urea.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **IV fluids with potassium chloride.**

elim: No red flags for surgery.
She is NBM with NG drainage; oral potassium will not be absorbed.
The obstruction has not resolved.
Feeding now would worsen vomiting.

steps.x: **B.** Rule: drip and suck means fluids AND electrolytes; low K also worsens ileus.

practice.stem: A 70 year old man has been treated for adhesional small bowel obstruction with an NG tube and IV fluids for 18 hours. His pain is now constant and severe. His temperature is 38.3°C, pulse rate 120 bpm and BP 104/66 mmHg. He has localised guarding. Repeat CT shows a closed loop with reduced bowel wall enhancement.
practice.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
o: Continue drip and suck for 48 hours
practice.e: Closed loop, ischaemia (poor enhancement, lactate 4.6) and peritonism mean urgent surgery. Continuing conservative care risks necrosis and perforation.

steps.x: Next step when conservative care has failed.

clues: closed loop with reduced bowel wall enhancement
steps.x: Closed loop and ischaemia: every indication for surgery.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Urgent laparotomy.**

elim: Waiting risks necrosis and perforation.
A flatus tube is for large bowel causes.
A contrast enema assesses the colon only.
A contrast study is for uncomplicated, non-settling adhesional SBO.

steps.x: **C. Urgent laparotomy.** Rule: red flags = theatre.

practice.stem: A 67 year old woman is 2 days after an open anterior resection. She has distension and nausea and has vomited once. Bowel sounds are absent and there is no colicky pain. practice.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
practice.e: Post-operative ileus with no transition point or leak is managed conservatively (NG if vomiting, IV fluids, correct potassium, reduce opioids) while motility recovers.

practice.stem: A 55 year old man has 1 day of colicky central abdominal pain coming in waves, with vomiting and distension. He had a laparotomy for trauma 8 years ago. On auscultation there are frequent high-pitched tinkling bowel sounds. CT confirms small bowel obstruction at a single transition point.
practice.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of his colicky pain and tinkling bowel sounds?
practice.e: Proximal bowel dilates with gas and fluid and contracts harder against the obstruction, causing colic and tinkling sounds until it fatigues.
